ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: No papers appeared to involve live data collection requiring an ethics approval statement.
ethics_check.report: We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 67 columns across 7 data files.
#### Issues Identified
2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Researchers increasingly share materials online, but often without a license, which means others cannot tell how they may reuse them.
Because materials often outlive their authors' involvement, reuse questions can go unanswered.
Licensing takes minutes, at the point of sharing or years later, and authors should act while they can still edit their materials.

Due to the increased adoption of open science practices across the behavioral sciences (see, e.g., Pfadt et al., 2025), sharing research materials, such as code or data, has become more common (Quintana, 2026).
text.formatted: Due to the increased adoption of open science practices across the behavioral sciences (see, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Pfadt et al., 2025)</ref>, sharing research materials, such as code or data, has become more common <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Quintana, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Open materials can help readers verify reported results and to build on them, for example by generating new hypotheses.
However, the open availability of materials does not guarantee that they can easily be reused.
One barrier to easy reuse is the poor organization of materials.

A recent analysis of articles in four prominent psychology journals (Cognition, Psychological Science, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Journal of Memory and Language), found that many of the associated repositories lacked documentation or had other shortcomings, such as hard-coded file locations, that make materials difficult to reuse (Quintana, 2026).

text.text: Only 27% (179/672, 95% CI = [23%, 30%]) of papers also contained license information with their shared materials (see Panel a of Figure 1).
text.formatted: Only 27% (179/672, 95% CI = [23%, 30%]) of papers also contained license information with their shared materials (see Panel a of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: This number increased from papers published in 2015 and 2020 to papers in 2025, which is driven by the increase at Psychological Science from 21% (95% CI = [15%, 30%]) to 91% (95% CI = [79%, 97%]).
This is likely due to a change in editorial policies starting in 2024, which ask authors to apply a license to shared materials (Hardwicke & Vazire, 2024).
text.formatted: This is likely due to a change in editorial policies starting in 2024, which ask authors to apply a license to shared materials <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Hardwicke & Vazire, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The majority (83%) of articles that applied a license used one of the two most common types, namely CC BY 4.0 or CC0 1.0 (see Panel b of Figure 1).
text.formatted: The majority (83%) of articles that applied a license used one of the two most common types, namely CC BY 4.0 or CC0 1.0 (see Panel b of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Both are permissive licenses that enable the most common forms of scholarly reuse.
This pattern matches the experience of two of the authors (B.S.S. and D.W.H.) in building openESM, a database of openly available experience sampling datasets (Siepe et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This pattern matches the experience of two of the authors (B.S.S. and D.W.H.) in building openESM, a database of openly available experience sampling datasets <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Siepe et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: More than half of the eligible datasets that we found were posted without a license, so we had to contact the repository owners.
Many of them were difficult or impossible to reach: some had moved institutions, others had left academia.
Seeking permission this way can sometimes work, but it is highly inefficient, and only possible if authors respond at all.
In our case, it hindered us from reusing data from thousands of participants.
This issue is especially timely in light of the August 2026 announcement from the Center for Open Science that all research projects on the OSF will become read-only in February 2027 (Nosek, 2026).
text.formatted: This issue is especially timely in light of the August 2026 announcement from the Center for Open Science that all research projects on the OSF will become read-only in February 2027 <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Nosek, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: From then on, project metadata can no longer be changed, which freezes the license status of all OSF projects (Open Science Framework Support, 2026), although registrations and preprints are not affected.
Consequently, all materials without a license will remain unlicensed, so reuse will require contacting owners for permission, which is time-consuming and often unsuccessful.
Researchers can draw on existing guidance when choosing a license.
For data and metadata, permissive Creative Commons licenses such as CC BY or CC0 are sensible defaults (The Turing

text.formatted: Panel a displays the share of articles with open research materials that had a license, comparing all papers published in 2015 & 2020 with those published in 2025.

text.text: We aggregated the first two years because only comparatively few articles were available in 2015, and it was unclear whether all of them had already selected a license on OSF, since OSF introduced license metadata that year.
Panel b displays the number of papers using each license; papers with several licenses count once per license; therefore, the total number of licenses is higher than the number of papers.
The full names of these licenses are available in our online supplement.
The online supplement includes a visualization with confidence intervals for all percentages.
Way Community, 2025), and were also the most common choices in our sample (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Way Community, 2025), and were also the most common choices in our sample (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Research software is better served by dedicated open-source licenses, such as the permissive MIT license or the copyleft GPL (Morin et al., 2012; The Turing Way Community, 2025).
text.formatted: Research software is better served by dedicated open-source licenses, such as the permissive MIT license or the copyleft GPL <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Morin et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">The Turing Way Community, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Some projects are more complex, for example, when a project mixes different forms of materials with some of them being under certain restrictions, or when an employer holds rights in the materials or has its own licensing policies.
However, these might be precisely the cases where potential reusers are most uncertain, so clarifying the terms of reusing is all the more worthwhile.
Academic librarians can typically provide licensing advice if needed.
OSF users, in particular, should check their existing projects before February 19, 2027, and set an appropriate license where necessary.
We have created a Shiny app (https://dsquintana.shinyapps.io/osf-license-check/) that automatically provides users with a list of their OSF projects and their associated licenses.
text.formatted: We have created a Shiny app (<ref type="url" target="https://dsquintana.shinyapps.io/osf-license-check/">https://dsquintana.shinyapps.io/osf-license-check/</ref>) that automatically provides users with a list of their OSF projects and their associated licenses.

text.text: There are also top-down approaches that can improve licensing practices.
For example, journals can require a license for shared materials by asking authors to state licensing information in their data availability statement.
The increase in OSF materials licensing at Psychological Science suggests that such requirements can have a substantial influence on licensing practices.
Repositories can also make license selection a mandatory step before materials are made public.
Some repositories, such as Zenodo (https://zenodo.org), already implement such a policy.
text.formatted: Some repositories, such as Zenodo (<ref type="url" target="https://zenodo.org">https://zenodo.org</ref>), already implement such a policy.

text.text: Another option for repositories is to provide a 'no license' option for users to select, so that the absence of a license reflects a deliberate decision instead of an oversight.
Shared materials often outlast their author's ability to manage them.
Platforms can change, and researchers often move institutions or leave academia altogether.
A license tells potential reusers what they may do without having to request direct permission from authors.
For most projects, adding a license takes a few minutes and should be part of every transparent research workflow.

text.text: Writing code such that it runs on another machine or carefully annotating all variables in a dataset can require substantial resources.
In contrast, applying a license typically only takes a few minutes, yet is a precondition for clarity about reuse conditions.
Given how little effort licensing usually takes, one might expect it to be standard practice.
However, despite existing guidance (e.g.,Morin et al., 2012;  The Turing Way Community, 2025), we regularly encounter unlicensed materials.
